newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Solana says Moscow has "misconceptions" about NATO.
newsitem.headline: Solana says Moscow has "misconceptions" about NATO.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Wednesday Russia had "misconceptions" about the alliance as the Kremlin stepped up its verbal barrage over the bloc's planned expansion eastwards.
"So far Russia has shown some interest. But there still remain many misconceptions and stereotypes in Russia's thinking about NATO," Solana told the Georgian parliament.
"If we are to make progress in overcoming them, they must be addressed head on and honestly."
At the same time Solana sought to reassure Russia, saying NATO wanted "enhanced cooperation" with Moscow and that it would not be left out of a new European security system.
"We know we will not be able to achieve increased security in Europe without Russia, let alone against it," he said.

Solana reiterated the alliance's promise that it would not place nuclear weapons on the territory of any new member states, saying: "NATO today does not pose a threat to anybody. It does not pose a threat to Russia."
Solana is on a tour of the former Soviet republics of Moldova, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He was speaking on the same day as President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary told Interfax news agency his trip had "an undeclared, behind-the-scenes" aim -- to prevent any form of integration between the former Soviet republics.
"The West as a whole and the leadership of NATO in particular, is opposed to any kind of integration between the newly independent states - the republics of the former USSR."

Solana's trip has clearly angered the Kremlin. Armenia and Georgia still have Russian military bases on their soil and the tinderbox Caucasus region as a whole is still seen as being a part of its shrinking geopolitical orbit.

None of the countries Solana visits are currently lobbying to join NATO, but leaders of Moldova and Georgian President Eduard Shevadnadze have said they would like to see a future European security system where the needs of small, officially non-aligned states can be enhanced.
Solana made clear that Russia's increasingly vitriolic crusade against the Western alliance would not bear fruit.
"These countries want to rejoin a Europe from which they were artificially separated. NATO's enlargement should be seen in the same light as the European Union expansion," he said.
Solana repeated vows that NATO would not base nuclear weapons in new member states.

"The alliance has no reason, no intention, and no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of the new members. NATO today does not pose a threat to anybody. It does not pose a threat to Russia," he said.

Solana said NATO was "seriously" ready to discuss the renegotiation of the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) agreement, one of the concessions Moscow wants to get from the West in the process of NATO's enlargement.
